name: MCP6004T-I_SL
title: MCP6001/1R/1U/2/4: 1 MHz, 100 µA rail-to-rail CMOS op amps, single, dual and quad
summary: A family of general-purpose CMOS operational amplifiers with a 1 MHz gain-bandwidth product and 90° phase margin, drawing about 100 µA per amplifier from a single 1.8 V to 6.0 V supply. Inputs and outputs swing rail to rail; the common-mode range runs 300 mV past each rail and the output does not reverse phase. MCP6001 (with pin variants R and U) is the single in SC-70-5 or SOT-23-5, MCP6002 the dual in PDIP, SOIC, MSOP or 2x3 DFN, and MCP6004 the quad in PDIP, SOIC or TSSOP; each comes in industrial (-40 °C to +85 °C) and extended (-40 °C to +125 °C) grades. MCP6004T-I/SL is the quad in 14-lead SOIC on tape and reel, industrial grade.
key_figures: 100 µA typ, 170 µA max per amplifier (VDD = 5.5 V)
within 25 mV of each rail (RL = 10 kΩ, VDD = 5.5 V)

notes: An order code is the device (a trailing T means tape and reel), a dash, the temperature letter (I or E), a slash and the package code: LT SC-70, OT SOT-23, MS MSOP, MC DFN, P PDIP, SN 8-lead SOIC, SL 14-lead SOIC, ST TSSOP.
The SC-70 package is offered for the MCP6001 alone; MCP6001R and MCP6001U come only in SOT-23.
MCP6001, MCP6001R and MCP6001U have different SOT-23-5 pin orders.
MCP6004T is listed with SOIC and MSOP; it should read SOIC and TSSOP (SL and ST), as the ordering examples MCP6004T-I/SL and MCP6004T-I/ST show.
The SN and SL SOIC body is given as 3.99 mm; it should read 3.90 mm, the E1 width on both package drawings.

circuits.title: Non-inverting amplifier
circuits.description: The signal drives the non-inverting input directly. R1 runs from the output back to the inverting input and R2 from that input to a reference voltage VREF, so the stage has a gain of 1 + R1/R2 about VREF. The amplifier runs between VDD and VSS.

parts.note: feedback resistor; sets the gain with R2

notes: Gain = 1 + R1/R2.

circuits.title: AC and DC test circuit
circuits.description: The bench circuit behind most of the DC and AC figures. Two matched 100 kΩ / 100 kΩ networks set a differential gain of 1 V/V: VP and VDD/2 feed the non-inverting input, VM and the output feed the inverting input, each 100 kΩ feedback leg with 6.8 pF beside it (to ground on the non-inverting side, across the resistor on the inverting side). Choosing VP and VM sets the common-mode voltage and the output level independently. The output is loaded with 10 kΩ to VL and 60 pF to ground; the supply is bypassed with 100 nF and 1 µF.
notes: GDM = RF/RG; VCM = (VP + VDD/2)/2; VOST = VIN– – VIN+; VOUT = (VDD/2) + (VP – VM) + VOST(1 + GDM).

circuits.title: Protecting the analog inputs
circuits.description: An amplifier with a series resistor in each input and R3 from the output back to the inverting input. R1 and R2 sit in series with the two inputs and cap the current an input can draw when it is pulled below VSS, where the internal ESD diodes conduct; D1 and D2, from each input up to VDD, stop the inputs rising too far above VDD and send that current into the supply, with R1 and R2 limiting it.
notes: D1 and D2 may also connect on the source side of R1 and R2; the diode current must then be limited some other way, R1 and R2 only limit inrush, and the DC current into VIN+ and VIN– stays very small.

circuits.title: Series output resistor for a capacitive load
circuits.description: A unity-gain follower driving a capacitive load CL through a small series resistor RISO. Feedback is taken at the amplifier pin, ahead of RISO, so the load looks resistive at high frequency and the loop keeps its phase margin. RISO is chosen from the recommended-RISO curve against CL divided by the noise gain.

circuits.title: Unused op amp, circuit A: buffered divider
circuits.description: One spare amplifier of an MCP6004 wired as a follower of a resistor divider across the supply. The amplifier sits at its lowest noise gain, its output holds still instead of toggling, and it delivers VREF = VDD × R2/(R1 + R2), any level inside the output range.

parts.note: one of the four amplifiers (section A pins shown)

notes: VREF = VDD × R2 / (R1 + R2).

circuits.title: Unused op amp, circuit B: inputs to the rails
circuits.description: One spare amplifier of an MCP6004 with its non-inverting input tied to VDD and its inverting input to ground, and its output left open. It needs no other parts and acts as a comparator, though it can draw more current than circuit A.

parts.note: one of the four amplifiers (section A pins shown)

circuits.title: Instrumentation amplifier with unity-gain buffer inputs
circuits.description: The two halves of an MCP6002 buffer VIN1 and VIN2 at unity gain. An MCP6001 with R1 = 20 kΩ and R2 = 10 kΩ forms the difference stage: VIN1's buffer drives its inverting input through R2 with R1 as feedback, and VIN2's buffer drives its non-inverting input through R2 with R1 to VREF. The output is (VIN2 – VIN1) × R1/R2 + VREF, a gain of 2 about VREF.
notes: VOUT = (VIN2 – VIN1) × R1/R2 + VREF.

circuits.title: Active second-order low-pass filter
circuits.description: A unity-gain Sallen-Key low-pass: 14.3 kΩ and 53.6 kΩ in series from the input to the non-inverting input, 33 pF from that input to ground, and 100 pF from the junction of the two resistors back to the output. The amplifier is a follower. It is a second-order Butterworth response, 100 kHz cutoff, unity gain (+1 V/V); the amplifier's 1 MHz bandwidth is only ten times the cutoff.

parts.note: from the resistor junction to the output

circuits.title: Peak detector with clear and sample CMOS analog switches
circuits.description: Amplifier A (half an MCP6002) drives diode D1 with its feedback taken from D1's cathode, so the output of D1 follows the input upward only; through RISO it charges C1, which holds the peak (VC1). Amplifier B, the other half, buffers VC1. When the sample switch closes, B charges C2 through a second RISO to VC2, and amplifier C (an MCP6001) buffers VC2 to the output. The clear switch discharges C1 through R1 to ground. Each clock cycle runs a sample time tSAMP, then a clear time tCLEAR, then a detect time tDETECT during which C1 collects the new peak.

parts.note: amplifier A (section A) and amplifier B (section B)
clear switch, C1 through R1 to ground

notes: The sample switch closes on the rising clock edge for tSAMP; the clear signal then closes the clear switch for tCLEAR; amplifier A then stores the peak of VIN on C1 for tDETECT.

operation.text: MCP6001 is a single amplifier, MCP6002 a dual and MCP6004 a quad; MCP6001R and MCP6001U are the single with other SOT-23-5 pin orders. All share one CMOS design: 1 MHz gain-bandwidth, 90° phase margin, 100 µA per amplifier, rail-to-rail inputs and outputs, and a supply of 1.8 V to 6.0 V. Each is offered in industrial (-40 °C to +85 °C) and extended (-40 °C to +125 °C) grades.

operation.topic: Phase margin with a capacitive load
operation.text: Phase margin is 90° typical, and 45° typical with a 500 pF load.
VDD sits 1.8 V to 6.0 V above VSS, and every other pin normally stays between the two. In single-supply use VSS goes to ground and VDD to the supply, which needs bypass capacitors.
On the DFN package the exposed pad is joined internally to VSS and must be tied to the same potential on the board.
The output does not reverse phase when an input goes beyond the supply rails.

ESD diodes guard each input: they clamp an input that falls more than a diode drop below VSS, and they also clamp inputs driven well above VDD, with a breakdown voltage that sits above the normal operating range and below the level of fast ESD events. The circuit around the part must keep input currents and voltages inside the absolute maximum ratings; series resistors limit the current when an input is pulled below ground, and external diodes to VDD stop it rising too far above. With the common-mode voltage below VSS the inputs can source sizeable current, so high-impedance circuits may need a narrower input range.

Two CMOS differential pairs work in parallel, one for low and one for high common-mode voltage, so the input range reaches 0.3 V beyond each rail. The changeover happens at VCM = VDD – 1.1 V; non-inverting circuits that need the best distortion and gain linearity should keep the input away from that level.
With RL = 10 kΩ to VDD/2 at VDD = 5.5 V the output swings to within 25 mV of each rail: VOH ≥ VDD – 25 mV and VOL ≤ VSS + 25 mV.

A growing load capacitance lowers phase margin and bandwidth, giving peaking in frequency and overshoot and ringing in time; the follower (G = +1) suffers most, but every gain behaves alike. Above roughly 100 pF at G = +1, a small resistor RISO in series with the output, outside the feedback loop, restores the margin, at some cost in bandwidth. RISO is picked from the recommended-RISO curve against CL/GN and then checked for peaking and overshoot on the bench or with the SPICE model.
Each VDD pin wants a local capacitor of 0.01 µF to 0.1 µF within 2 mm, plus a bulk capacitor of 1 µF or more within 100 mm; nearby analog parts may share the bulk capacitor.

A spare amplifier of the MCP6004 should be wired as circuit A (a follower of a divider, at minimum noise gain) or circuit B (inputs tied to the rails, fewest parts, possibly more current), so its output does not toggle and couple into its neighbours.

Where bias current matters, surface leakage on the board counts: at low humidity nearby traces typically show about 10^12 Ω, so 5 V between them drives 5 pA, more than the 1 pA typical bias current at 25 °C. A guard ring around the sensitive pins, held at their voltage, cuts it. In a follower or non-inverting stage the guard ring goes to VIN– (the common-mode voltage) and VIN+ is reached by a wire off the board surface. In an inverting or transimpedance stage, such as a photodetector amplifier, the guard ring goes to VIN+ (the reference, e.g. VDD/2 or ground) and VIN– is reached by a wire off the board surface.

The pA bias current allows large resistors and small capacitors in active filters, at the cost of more resistor noise and more effect from parasitic capacitance. Good practice puts the amplifier bandwidth at 100 times the cutoff or more; ten times works but leaves the response more sensitive to component tolerances. The 100 kHz example values came from the FilterLab design tool.

Charging of C1 and C2 is limited by the amplifier source current and discharging by τ = R1 × C1; tDETECT depends on how fast the input changes. When the input drops below VC1, D1 turns off, the loop opens and amplifier A saturates; when the input rises again, A recovers at its slew rate. The storage capacitors should be below 40 µF, with RISO chosen as for any capacitive load, so that slew rate does not set the speed.
